# Pacific Crest Space Force Annex — conveyance study for the 13.8 kV site distribution

You are the electrical engineer and cost estimator of the design-build contractor for solicitation FA4610-26-R-0031 at
Pacific Crest Space Force Annex, Los Angeles County, California. The Government requires a **conveyance study**
before the 35 % design: for seven medium-voltage circuits — from the site substation SS-1 to the medium-voltage
switchgear lineups of the Mission Support Facility MB-1, to the Central Utility Plant CUP-1, to the gate house and to
the lift station, from CUP-1 to warehouse W-3, and inside MB-1 from switchgear MSG-A to unit substation USS-A1 — decide
which conveyance is the most cost-effective one that the governing criteria permit, design it, and price every
conveyance type the study must evaluate.

The contract documents are in this workspace: the RFP section with the study requirements, labor classification
plan and estimating basis; the installation electrical design standard; the governing DoD criteria and guide
specifications; federal regulations; the site utility plan, one-line diagram, building plans, utility survey and tree survey; the
geotechnical report and boring logs; the protective device settings schedule; cable data, the approved cable
submittal and ampacity tables; the labor-unit database, crew book and payroll burden; supplier, rental and
subcontract quotes; wage determinations; equipment rate schedules; escalation and producer price indexes; and the
Government estimate template. Some folders hold superseded material; the transmittal says what is current and the
installation standard sets the order of precedence. Government-furnished documents are not guaranteed free of
errors — the RFP requires the study to report the ones you find. The NFPA 70, IEEE C2 and NECA texts are not
provided; the project is governed by the documents provided.

## What to deliver

A study package for all seven circuits (items `C01` … `C07`, defined in RFP Section 01 11 00):

1. **For every item, every conveyance type the study must evaluate** (RFP 1.4): whether the governing criteria permit
   it for this circuit and the clause that decides, its take-off, labor hours, the labor, equipment and material
   rates used, its direct cost, the estimate roll-up to total project cost, and its cost per linear foot.
2. **For every item, the recommended conveyance designed** so that it can be built as priced: the route on the site
   (or building) plan, each segment's installation method, burial depth, duct arrangement and spares, reinforcement,
   trench protective system and dewatering; manholes, poles and pull boxes with their positions; the cable size and
   number of parallel sets from the ampacity at the governing installation condition; the cable pulling calculation
   of every pull.
3. **A study report** (`conveyance_study_report.md`, `.pdf` or `.docx`) presenting, per item, the recommendation and
   the tables of labor hours, rates used and cost per linear foot of each conveyance type evaluated.

Among designs the criteria permit, the one with the lower total project cost, estimated by the RFP estimating basis,
is the better design.

## Coordinates

Site feet as drawn on C-101 (DXF): `x` = easting, `y` = northing. The MB-1 electrical plan E-101 uses the same frame.

## Deliverable format

Write `output/submission.zip` containing `conveyance_study.xlsx` and the report at the zip root. Use the sheet names
and header row of `templates/conveyance_study_TEMPLATE.xlsx` (header in row 1, one record per row; extra columns are
ignored). Types, methods and codes are those of the RFP and the cost documents: conveyance types `CEDB`, `UEDB`,
`DBC`, `HDD`, `OH` (site items) and `RMC`, `EMT`, `TRAY-EN`, `TRAY-LD` (item C05); segment methods `CE`
(concrete-encased ductbank), `UE` (conduit without encasement), `DB` (direct-buried cable), `HDD`, `JB`
(jack-and-bore rigid steel conduit), `JS` (jack-and-sleeve), `OH` (overhead span), and for C05 `RMC`, `EMT`,
`TRAY-EN`, `TRAY-LD`; take-off codes are the labor-unit database codes, the supplier quote item codes, and `SUB-HDD`,
`SUB-JB`, `SUB-JS` for the subcontract quotes (dollars in `subcontract_usd`).

**Items** — one row per item: `item_id`, `recommended_type`, `cable_size` (AWG/kcmil as in the cable data, blank if
none), `sets`, `overhead_conductor` (ACSR size, blank if none), `design_current_a`, `ampacity_per_set_a` (at the
governing condition), `route_length_ft`, `total_project_cost_usd`, `cost_per_lf_usd`.

**Segments** — the recommended route of each item, one row per segment in order from the source end:
`item_id`, `seg_no`, `method`, `route` (polyline `x1,y1; x2,y2; …`; consecutive segments share end points),
`cover_in` (finished grade to the top of the duct envelope, conduit or cable; blank for OH and C05), `duct_rows`,
`duct_cols`, `duct_size_in`, `spare_ducts`, `shared_with` (other items whose circuits occupy the same ductbank on this
segment, comma-separated), `reinforced` (`Y`/`N`), `soil_type` (OSHA `A`/`B`/`C`), `protective_system` (`none`,
`slope` or `box`), `slope_h_per_v`, `dewatering` (`Y`/`N`).

**Structures** — manholes, poles and pull boxes of the recommended designs: `item_id`, `structure_id`, `kind`
(`MH`, `POLE`, `RISER_POLE`, `PULLBOX`), `x_ft`, `y_ft` (on the route), `pole_height_ft`, `guys`, `dead_end` (`Y`/`N`),
`protective_system`, `slope_h_per_v` (manhole excavations).

**Pulls** — every cable pull of the recommended designs: `item_id`, `pull_id`, `from_id`, `to_id` (structure ids, or
`START` / `END` for the item's terminals), `length_ft`, `max_tension_lb`, `max_sidewall_lb_per_ft`, `jam_ratio`,
`fill_pct`. A vertex of an underground route that is not a structure is a field long-sweep bend.

**Alternatives** — one row per item and conveyance type evaluated: `item_id`, `type`, `admissible` (`Y`/`N`),
`governing_clause` (document and clause that permits or excludes it), `length_ft`, `labor_mh`, `labor_usd`,
`equipment_usd`, `material_usd`, `subcontract_usd`, `direct_cost_usd`, `jooh_usd`, `hooh_usd`, `profit_usd`,
`bond_usd`, `escalation_usd`, `contract_cost_usd`, `contingency_usd`, `sioh_usd`, `total_project_cost_usd`,
`cost_per_lf_usd`, `recommended` (`Y` on exactly one row per item).

**Takeoff** — the priced lines behind every alternative: `item_id`, `type`, `code`, `quantity`, `unit`, `labor_mh`,
`labor_usd`, `equipment_usd`, `material_usd`, `subcontract_usd`.

**LaborRates** — `class` (crew book position), `wd_group`, `classification`, `base_usd`, `fringe_usd`, `burden_pct`,
`loaded_rate_usd`. **EquipmentRates** — `equipment_id`, `description`, `source`, `hourly_rate_usd`.

**Markups** — `parameter`, `value` for `jooh_pct`, `hooh_pct`, `profit_pct`, `bond_rate_pct`, `escalation_factor`,
`contingency_pct`, `sioh_pct`, `area_cost_factor_applied` (the factor applied to the estimate, `1` if none) and
`wage_determination` (number and modification used).

**Register** — the requirements you applied: `req_id`, `document` (number/title, with revision where documents have
several), `clause` (section, paragraph, table or figure), `requirement`, `value`, `applies_to`.

**Findings** — every error or inconsistency found in the Government-furnished documents: `finding_id`, `document`,
`location`, `defect` (with the conflicting values), `correction` (what you used).

### Live formulas

In **Alternatives**, `direct_cost_usd` through `cost_per_lf_usd` must be formulas referencing the cells they are
computed from (and the **Markups** values), and in **LaborRates** `loaded_rate_usd` must be a formula; the reviewer
recalculates the workbook and changes inputs to confirm the results follow. Use ordinary arithmetic and common
functions (`SUM`, `SUMIFS`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `ROUND`, `IF`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `VLOOKUP`) with plain cell references. No
spreadsheet application is installed in this workspace; Python with `openpyxl` is, and a workbook written by it without
cached values is acceptable, because the reviewer evaluates the formulas itself.

## How the package is judged

Each item is judged separately. Every requirement is recomputed from the project documents, the site geometry and
your submitted design. The take-off, labor hours, dollars and total project cost of the recommended conveyance are
compared with the estimate recomputed from its geometry by the RFP estimating basis; the arithmetic of the other
alternatives is checked from your own take-off. Engineering tolerances apply (about 3 % for quantities, pulling results
and the recommended conveyance's hours and dollars, 2 % for rates and roll-up arithmetic, 0.02 percentage point for
markup percentages). There is no minimum or maximum number of register or findings rows.


## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace — the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

Department of the Air Force - Pacific Crest Space Force Annex, Civil Engineer Squadron                  PCSFA-IEDS Rev 3 2026-05-01




 PCSFA-IEDS Installation Electrical Design Standard - Revision 3
 Pacific Crest Space Force Annex, Los Angeles County, California. Issued 2026-05-01. Supersedes Revision 2
 (2024-03-15).

 1 GENERAL

 1.1 Applicability. This standard applies to new and modified electrical distribution on the installation. It supplements the
 Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC) and Unified Facilities Guide Specifications (UFGS) named in the project documents; it does
 not repeat them. The project is a Department of the Air Force project: the Air Force requirements and notes of the UFC
 apply.
 1.2 Referenced documents. UFC 3-550-01 (2016, Change 3), UFC 3-520-01 (2025), UFC 3-501-01 (2024), UFC 3-301-01
 (2023, Change 5), UFC 3-740-05 (2022, Change 1), UFS 3-701-01 (2026), UFGS 33 71 02, UFGS 33 71 01, UFGS 26 20
 00, UFGS 31 00 00, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, EP 1110-1-8.
 1.3 Order of precedence. Where project documents differ, the following order governs: (1) the project-specific requirements
 of this standard, where they are stricter than the criteria; (2) the UFC; where a UFC and a UFGS section state different limits
 for the same concern, the stricter limit; (3) approved project submittals, which govern over manufacturers' general catalogue
 data; (4) the current protective device settings schedule, which governs over device ratings shown on one-line diagrams; (5)
 the subsurface utility engineering (SUE) survey, which governs over record utility locations and depths shown on drawings;
 (6) boring logs and laboratory results, which govern over summary tables of geotechnical reports; (7) the arborist tree
 survey, which governs over trees shown on drawings.

 2 SYSTEM

 2.1 The installation primary distribution is 13.8 kV, resistance grounded, 3-phase 3-wire. Medium-voltage cable:
 single-conductor Type MV-105, XLPE insulation, 133 % insulation level, copper tape shield, aluminum conductor (UFC
 3-550-01 3-11.1.2, 3-11.8). Minimum size 1/0 AWG. Three single conductors of a circuit (a set) are installed together in one
 duct or raceway.
 2.2 Design current. The ampacity of a medium-voltage feeder (ampacity of one set at the governing installation condition
 times the number of parallel sets) shall not be less than the phase pickup setting of the feeder's protective device.
 2.3 Load factor for ampacity. Mission feeders F1 and F2 from SS-1: 100 %. All other feeders: 75 %.
 2.4 Short-circuit withstand. Each set of medium-voltage cable shall withstand the full available fault current of its source bus
 for the backup (breaker-failure) clearing time, both as stated in the current protective device settings schedule: the
 conductor short-circuit capability tabulated by the cable manufacturer for the tabulated duration equal to or next longer than
 the clearing time shall not be less than the available fault current.

 4 SITE DISTRIBUTION

 4.1 Conveyance selection follows UFC 3-550-01 paragraph 3-11 and this chapter. Overhead distribution is not permitted
 inside the industrial area delineated on C-101 (Area Development Plan 2024, a congested industrial area) or within the W-3
 dock crane operating area; outside them overhead lines are permitted, with underground risers to pad-mounted equipment
 and buildings.
 4.2 Primary circuits between underground structures, and between underground structures and equipment, shall be
 concrete-encased ductbanks (UFC 3-550-01 3-11.2.1; UFGS 33 71 02 3.7.9). Direct-buried cable and conduit without
 concrete encasement are not permitted for the installation's primary distribution.
 4.3 Existing pavement. Perimeter Road, Mission Drive and the MB-1 access drive shall not be open-cut; cross them by
 directional bore or jack-and-bore (UFC 3-550-01 3-11.2.2). Parking lot P-1 and the CUP-1 service yard may be saw-cut and
 patched; ductbanks under them shall be reinforced, and the encasement shall extend at least 5 ft beyond the edges of the
 paving (UFGS 33 71 02 3.7.8.1). Directional bores are used only for the crossings listed in UFC 3-550-01 3-11.4.1 (roads,
 parking lots, bodies of water); a bore shall not extend more than 50 ft beyond the pavement edge or channel bank on either
 side. Channel DC-1 shall not be open-cut.
 4.4 Redundancy. Conveyances of SS-1 bus A feeders (F1, F3) and bus B feeders (F2, F4) shall not share ductbanks or
 underground structures and shall be at least 20 ft apart (centerline to centerline), except within 50 ft of the SS-1 fence or of
 the MB-1 walls.


Installation Electrical Design Standard                                                                                      Page 1
 Department of the Air Force - Pacific Crest Space Force Annex, Civil Engineer Squadron                    PCSFA-IEDS Rev 3 2026-05-01




 4.5 Rail spur RR-SPUR-2 remains in service. Conduits crossing it shall be jacked rigid galvanized steel conduit where the
 crossing length is 50 ft or less, and jack-and-sleeve otherwise (UFGS 33 71 02 3.7.4). The crossing length is the length of
 conduit within 12 ft of the outer rails. Top of conduit not less than 50 in below top of rail; top of rail is 8 in above finished
 grade.
 4.6 Ampacity basis. Use the cable manufacturer's ampacity tables with their selection rules. The soil thermal resistivity at a
 location is that of the nearest boring (geotechnical report); the earth ambient temperature is 25 C; the earth ambient
 correction factors apply to every underground table (ductbank, single conduit in earth, direct burial). The number of circuits
 in a ductbank is the number of occupied ducts (all items); spare ducts are not counted. The governing ampacity of a feeder
 is the lowest along its underground route. Directional bores and jacked crossings are excluded from the governing condition
 where their total length is not more than 25 percent of the underground run (UFC 3-550-01 B-2.1). Overhead conductors:
 ACSR tables at 40 C ambient. Building raceways and cable trays: 40 C ambient.
 4.7 Directional bores: UFC 3-550-01 Appendix B (HDPE SDR 11, cover, conduit fill). Cover under pavement 48 in and
 elsewhere 120 in, except within 10 ft of either end of the bore.
 4.8 Ductbanks: Type EB-20 PVC in concrete encasement, 5 in minimum duct, 3 in spacing and 3 in cover (UFC 3-550-01
 3-11.2.1, 3-11.2.2); spare ducts per UFC 3-550-01 3-11.2.2 rounded up to whole ducts; one 4/0 AWG bare copper ground
 conductor per ductbank (UFGS 33 71 02 3.7.1); minimum cover per UFC 3-550-01 3-11.2.2 and UFGS 33 71 02 3.7.9,
 stricter governs.
 4.9 Overhead lines (installation practice). Maximum span: 1/0 ACSR 300 ft, 3/0 ACSR 280 ft, 336.4 ACSR 250 ft, 477 ACSR
 220 ft. Poles: wood, Class 3, 45 ft; both poles of a span crossing a road: 50 ft. Guy every pole where the line deflects more
 than 5 degrees; dead-end with two guys where it deflects more than 60 degrees; riser poles are dead-ends with one guy.
 Poles not less than 25 ft from buildings and 6 ft from road edges, not in pavement, within 12 ft of the rail, or within the
 channel buffer. Setting depth per UFGS 33 71 01 3.1.3.1. Conductor design tension per UFC 3-550-01 3-10.
 4.10 Underground structures: UFC 3-550-01 3-11.5 and 3-11.6, including the Air Force distances of 3-11.5.5; manholes are
 not placed in pavement. A pulling calculation submitted in the pulling plan for a pull is the calculation that permits the greater
 distances of 3-11.6 for that pull. Changes of direction without a manhole use field long-sweep bends of 25 ft radius; the
 straight lengths on both sides of the bend shall accommodate the bend tangent. Standard manhole: precast 6 ft x 8 ft x 7 ft
 (circuits up to 15 kV).
 4.11 Cable pulling (UFC 3-501-01 3-2.11; UFGS 33 71 02 3.3). Pulling tension and sidewall bearing pressure limits per the
 approved cable submittal. Each pull runs between consecutive structures or terminals and may be made in either direction.
 Vertical riser elbows at equipment terminals and riser poles: 90 degrees, 36 in radius. Building raceway elbows: 36 in
 radius; cable tray fittings: 24 in radius.
 4.12 Excavation (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P). Classify the soil at an excavation from the log of the nearest boring (Appendix
 A), taking the least stable layer within the excavation depth; granular soils and soils below groundwater are Type C.
 Excavations 5 ft or deeper require a protective system: sloping not steeper than Appendix B for the soil type, or a trench
 shield. Manhole excavations are 8 ft deep. Dewater excavations extending below groundwater.
 4.13 Existing utilities: horizontal separation 5 ft edge to edge where parallel, vertical separation 12 in at crossings.
 4.14 Tree protection. Retained trees of the arborist tree survey have a tree protection zone of radius 1 ft per inch of trunk
 diameter (DBH), measured from the trunk. No trench, manhole, pole or other excavation may lie within a tree protection
 zone. Conduits may pass beneath a zone only by directional bore or jack-and-bore with not less than 48 in cover; the
 Activity approves such bores as crossings of an environmentally sensitive area (UFC 3-550-01 3-11.4.1). Trees the survey
 marks for removal are not protected.

 5 BUILDING DISTRIBUTION

 5.1 Medium-voltage cable inside buildings: UFC 3-520-01 Table 3-1 and UFGS 26 20 00 3.1.6 and 3.1.8. Required vertical
 space: cable tray 6 in plus 12 in access headroom; rigid conduit 6 in. Available space per room: A-501 schedule. No
 conveyance within 10 ft of the SCIF (IT-1) walls. Rises at MSG-A and USS-A1: 7 ft each, with a 90-degree elbow.
 5.2 Penetrations: rigid conduit is firestopped at every fire-rated wall. Cable tray stops 10 in from 2-hour walls and the cables
 pass through 4 in rigid steel sleeves extending 12 in on each side, filled not more than 40 percent (UFGS 26 20 00 3.1.8);
 tray crossing 1-hour walls is firestopped as a rigid conduit penetration per set.
 5.3 Supports: tray every 6 ft (UFGS 26 20 00 3.1.8), rigid conduit every 10 ft. Seismic bracing (UFC 3-301-01 design
 memorandum DM-26-04): transverse braces every 40 ft and longitudinal braces every 80 ft of run. Pull boxes so that bends

 1. Construction
 Conductor: compact stranded aluminum, alloy 1350. Conductor shield: extruded semiconducting thermoset. Insulation:
 cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE), 133 percent insulation level for 15 kV systems. Insulation shield: extruded
 semiconducting thermoset, free stripping. Metallic shield: helically applied bare copper tape with overlap. Jacket: black
 sunlight-resistant polyvinyl chloride (PVC). Single conductor. Rated conductor temperature 90 C normal operation, 130 C
 emergency, 250 C short circuit.

 2. Applications
 For use on 5 kV through 15 kV grounded and ungrounded systems in wet or dry locations, installed in conduit, underground
 duct systems, direct burial, cable tray and aerial messenger supported installations.

 Weights and diameters are nominal values per single conductor and are subject to manufacturing tolerances of +/- 5 percent.

 4. Installation Data
 4.1 Maximum pulling tension. When pulling with a pulling eye attached to the conductors, the maximum pulling tension is
 0.006 lb per circular mil of aluminum conductor area. When three single conductors are pulled together, the allowable
 tension is calculated on the cross-sectional area of two conductors only (the load is not assumed to be shared equally by
 the third conductor). The allowable tension shall not exceed 10,000 lb with a pulling eye in any case.

 4.2 Maximum sidewall bearing pressure. The maximum sidewall bearing pressure (SWBP) at any bend is 1,000 lb/ft of
 bend radius.

 4.3 Coefficients of dynamic friction. The following values apply to well-lubricated pulls with a pulling compound
 compatible with the PVC jacket.
                          Raceway                                                         Coefficient of friction f
                          PVC conduit (Type EB-20, Schedule 40)                           0.35
                          HDPE conduit (SDR 11)                                           0.30
                          Rigid galvanized steel conduit / EMT                            0.40
                          Cable tray with rollers                                         0.15


 4.4 Configuration of three cables in a conduit. Let d = cable outside diameter and D = conduit inside diameter. Use the
 triangular configuration when D/d < 2.8; use the cradled configuration otherwise. Weight correction factor wc:
      Cradled: wc = 1 + (4/3) x ( d / (D - d) )^2

      Triangular: wc = 1 / sqrt( 1 - ( d / (D - d) )^2 )

 4.5 Jamming. Avoid conduit-to-cable diameter ratios D/d between 2.8 and 3.2; in this range the cables can wedge in bends.

 4.6 Conduit fill. The total cross-sectional area of the cables shall not exceed 40 percent of the conduit internal area.

 4.7 Pulling tension calculation. Calculate the tension section by section in the direction of pull, where T1 = tension
 entering the section (lb), T2 = tension leaving the section (lb), f = coefficient of friction, W = total weight of the three cables
 (lb/ft), L = section length (ft), theta = bend angle (radians) and e = base of natural logarithms:
      Straight horizontal section: T2 = T1 + wc x f x W x L

      Horizontal bend: T2 = T1 x e^(wc x f x theta)

 Assume a feed-in tension of 100 lb at the reel for the first section. Calculate in both directions and pull from the end giving
 the lower tension.

 1. Introduction
 This report presents the results of the geotechnical investigation performed for the new underground and overhead 13.8 kV
 site distribution serving the Mission Support Facility MB-1, the Central Utility Plant CUP-1 and outlying loads. The purpose
 of the investigation was to characterize the subsurface soils along the anticipated conveyance corridors, provide soil thermal
 resistivity data for cable ampacity calculations, and provide information for excavation planning, backfill and pavement
 restoration.

 2. Site Description and Published Soil Information
 The site is a developed, generally level industrial area with buildings, paved roads and parking, an active rail spur and an
 open drainage channel along the eastern portion of the site. Finished grades range from approximately elevation 39 to 44 ft.
 Coordinates in this report are in site grid feet consistent with drawing C-101.

 The site lies within NRCS map unit 2478607, Urban land-Thums-Windfetch complex, 0 to 2 percent slopes (Los Angeles
 County, California, Southeastern Part, survey area CA696). The map unit is composed of Urban land (50 percent), Thums
 (20 percent) and Windfetch (15 percent) soils with minor components. The Thums and Windfetch components are well
 drained to moderately well drained clay loams with argillic subsoil horizons; the published risk of corrosion of uncoated steel
 is High. Published map-unit data are generalized and do not replace the site specific boring information.
 Source: Soil Survey Staff, Natural Resources Conservation Service, United States Department of Agriculture. Soil Survey Geographic (SSURGO)
 Database, accessed through Soil Data Access. The USDA-NRCS is acknowledged as the data source.


 3. Field Exploration Program
 Twelve borings (B-1 through B-12) were drilled between 2025-04-07 and 2025-04-10 with a truck-mounted drill rig using 8 in
 hollow-stem augers to a depth of 15 ft below existing grade. Standard penetration tests were performed at 2.5 ft intervals to
 10 ft and at 5 ft intervals thereafter; relatively undisturbed samples were recovered in cohesive soils. Soils were logged in
 the field by a staff geologist and classified in accordance with the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS). Boring
 locations were surveyed with RTK GNSS. Boreholes were backfilled with bentonite grout and patched at the surface.
 Individual boring logs are presented in Appendix A and in electronic form (files B-01.csv to B-12.csv).

 9. Backfill and Pavement Restoration
 On-site lean clay free of debris may be reused as general trench backfill above the select backfill zone, placed in loose lifts
 not exceeding 8 in and compacted to at least 90 percent of maximum dry density (95 percent within 2 ft of pavement
 subgrade), at moisture content near optimum. Imported sand used as bedding or thermal backfill should be clean, well
 graded and free of organic matter. Where pavement is removed, restore with a section at least equal to the existing section.

 10. Limitations
 The conclusions in this report are based on the borings at the locations shown and on the laboratory test results.
 Subsurface conditions between and beyond the borings may differ. This report was prepared for the design of the project

cd /filesystem/final_batch4__electrical_task12_conveyance_study__blind && for F in 00_admin/Attachment_J-3_Wage_Determination_CA20260022_Mod2.txt 50_cost/wage_determinations/CA20260022_Mod5_2026-08-06.txt; do echo "######## $F"; head -30 $F | grep -A8 "Modification"; python3 - "$F" <<'EOF'
import sys,re
txt=open(sys.argv[1]).read()
# split into blocks by dashed lines
blocks=txt.split('----------------------------------------------------------------')
for b in blocks:
    hdr=re.search(r'^\s*([A-Z]{4}\d{4}-\d{3})\s+(\S+)',b,re.M)
    if not hdr: continue
    if hdr.group(1) not in ('ELEC1245-001','ELEC0011-004','LABO0300-003','ENGI0012-024'): continue
    print('==',hdr.group(1),hdr.group(2))
    # find rates
    for m in re.finditer(r'([A-Z][^\$]*?)\.{2,}\s*\$\s*([\d\.]+)\s+([\d\.]+)',b,re.S):
        name=' '.join(m.group(1).split())
        print('   ',name[:90],'|',m.group(2),m.group(3))
EOF

11-2.1        Weighted Guidelines Method.

The weighted guidelines method yields a reasonable profit value and is to be used on
contracts that include profit. This methodology is to be used wherever a detailed direct
costing method is used for preparing cost estimates. A rate of profit may be used based
on historical experience for early-stage cost estimates prepared for programming,
budgeting, reconnaissance, or concept design.

11-2.2        Weighted Guideline Factors for the Alternate Structured Approach.

Based on the circumstances of each procurement action, each of the factors listed in
the “Guidelines for Weighted Factors Profit Determination”, at \1\
https://www.wbdg.org/dod/ufc/ufc-3-740-05, /1/ will be weighted from 0.03 to 0.12 as
discussed in the following text. Statements in sufficient detail to explain the reasons for
assigning the specific weights shall be included on the profit computation sheet. The
value will then be obtained by multiplying the rate column by the weight column. The
value column when totaled indicates the fair and reasonable profit percentage.

         •    Degree of Risk. Where the work involves no risk or the degree of risk is
              very small, the weighting is 0.03; as the degree of risk increases, the
              weighting is increased up to a maximum of 0.12. Lump sum items will
              have, generally, a higher weighted value than unit price items for which
              quantities are provided. Other things to consider include the nature of
              work; where the work is to be performed; the reasonableness of
              negotiated costs; the amount of labor included in the costs; and whether
              the negotiation occurs before or after the period of performance of work.

                                            49
                                                                           UFC 3-740-05
                                                                     09 December 2022
                                                           Change 1, 20 November 2025

          •   Relative Difficulty of Work. If the work is difficult and complex, the
              weighting is 0.12 and is proportionately reduced to 0.03 for simple jobs.
              This factor is tied in to some extent with the degree of risk. Some things
              to consider include the technical nature of the work; by whom work is to be
              done; location of work; and time schedule.
          •   Size of the Job. Work not more than $100,000 will be weighted at 0.12.
              Work estimated between $100,000 and $5,000,000 will be proportionately
              weighted from 0.12 to 0.05. Work from $5,000,000 to $10,000,000 shall
              be weighted at 0.04 and work in excess of $10,000,000 at 0.03.
          •   Period of Performance. Jobs exceeding 24 months are to be weighted at
              0.12. Jobs of lesser duration are to be proportionately weighted to a
              minimum of 0.03 for jobs not to exceed 30 days. No weight is given for
              modification cost estimates when additional performance time is not
              required.
          •   Contractor’s Investment. Jobs are to be weighted from 0.03 to 0.12, with
              lower values representing lower degrees of contractor investment (below
              average) and higher values representing higher degrees (above average).
              Things to consider include amount of subcontracting; mobilization
              payment item; Government-furnished property; method of making
              progress payments; and front-end requirements of the job.
          •   Assistance by Government. Jobs are to be weighted from 0.12 to 0.03
              from below average to above average. Things to consider include use of
              Government-owned property, equipment and facilities, and expediting
              assistance.
          •   Subcontracting. Jobs are to be weighted inversely proportional to the
              amount of subcontracting. Where 80 percent or more of the work is to be
              subcontracted, the weighting is to be 0.03 and such weighting
              proportionately increased to 0.12 where work is primarily performed by the
              prime contractor's own forces.

11-2.3        Separate Profit Calculation.

A separate profit calculation is to be performed for the prime contractor and for each
subcontractor. When the subcontractor assumes the risk and responsibility for portions
of the work, the prime contractor's profit rate on that work is decreased. Generally, profit
is applied as a percentage rate to the total of costs required by the contract or
modification scope. For early design stage cost estimates, a rate of profit may be
assumed based on past historical experience.

pulling tension or site requirements, separation of up to 600 ft (180 m) is permitted.

Pull boxes are used for electric circuits supplying low-voltage electric loads which
require conductors no larger than 1/0 AWG and no more than one 2-inch (52 mm)
conduit entrance at each side. Wherever larger conduits are installed, use handholes or
manholes. Do not use pull boxes in areas subject to vehicular traffic.

Comply with NEMA WC 74 and select type MV (105°C) aluminum or copper based on
the specific applications as defined in Para. 3-11.1. Provide a 600 volt insulated neutral
when required. For the Army and Air Force, concentric neutral conductors are also
authorized.

               paper insulated lead covered (PILC) for new installations.

               classified as multi-grounded (4 wire systems throughout the entire circuit).

               shielded cables only where existing manholes are utilized and the

approved/listed for electrical system installations, and minimum Schedule 80 meeting

Note: Install HDPE conduit below freeze lines and in no case can the conduit be

B-1.1            Conduit Design – 1,000 Volts to 34,500 Volts.

Provide a minimum size HDPE conduit of 5 inches (130 mm) for distribution voltages
greater than 1,000 V and less than 34.5 kV (nominal). Do not exceed 30 percent
conduit fill.

Install HDPE conduit with a minimum ground cover of:

        •    120 inches (3 m) in non-pavement-covered areas.
        •    48 inches (1.2 m) in pavement-covered areas.

B-1.2            Conduit Design – Less Than 1,000 Volts.

Provide a minimum size HDPE conduit of 4 inches (100 mm) for distribution voltages
less than 1,000 V. Do not exceed 35 percent conduit fill.

Install HDPE conduit with a minimum ground cover of 48 inches (1.2 m) in pavement- or
non-pavement-covered areas.

B-1.3            Conduit Design – Branch Circuit Wiring Less Than 600 Volts.

Provide a minimum size HDPE conduit for branch circuit wiring less than 600 V that is
determined by calculation, addressing, as a minimum, branch circuit conductor size,
maximum allowable pulling tension, and maximum 5 percent voltage drop. Do not
exceed 40 percent conduit fill.

Install HDPE conduit with a minimum ground cover of 24 inches (610 mm) min
pavement- or non-pavement-covered areas.

B-2              INSTALLATION METHODS.

The use of specific conductor or insulation types for either high- or low-voltage
installations is not mandated here. However, the combination of a chosen conductor
and insulation type may not meet the requirements for the installation methods required
in the following paragraphs where length, depth, and routing of the directional bore
conduit may require an alternative conductor material and/or insulation type (i.e.,
maximum pulling tensions are different for aluminum and copper conductors).

                                                           Change 3, 01 November 2019
B-2.1             Ampacity.

If the directional bored portion of the cable run is more than 25 percent of the total run
length, evaluate and document the conductor derated ampacity in accordance with
NFPA 70 Article 310.60 (C) (2).

B-2.2             Installation.

Water-jetting is not permitted. Use drilling fluids for DB methods that are approved by
federal, state, and local codes and authorized for use by the BCE.

Pre-installed cable-in-conduit is not permitted. Install the conduit(s) immediately after
the conduit hole is completed.

B-2.3             Allowable Pulling Tension.

B-2.3.1           Distance.

There is no restriction on DB distances provided the allowable pulling tension of the
conduit and installed conductors are not exceeded, conductor splices are not within the
conduit, and maximum ampacity of conductors due to depth derating is not exceeded.

B-2.3.2           Calculation Requirements.

A registered Professional Engineer (PE) must calculate pulling tension requirements for
each directional bore, taking into consideration the HDPE conduit(s) size and type, bend
radius, elevation changes, vertical and horizontal path deviations, installed electrical
conductor size and type, and any conductor ampacity derating due to depth of HDPE
conduit. The electrical contractor must provide certification of compliance with the PE‘s
design requirements.

The professional engineering design process must include consideration of tensile
forces and bend radii created during the installation so that allowable limits are not
exceeded. Allowable tensile forces must be determined by a PE, including accounting
for the conduit’s allowable bend radius to prevent ovalization and kinking from
installation. Do not exceed 5 percent ovalization of the conduit.

B-2.4             Termination into Equipment Pads.

Terminate HDPE conduits into concrete-pad-mounted electrical equipment from either a
pavement or non-pavement transitional area as indicated in Figures B-1 through B-5.

conductor exiting the conduit is bent past the vertical plane formed with the equipment
pad when routed to conductor terminations and with approved insulated bushings

2.20. Operating Cost Elements. The total operating cost is the sum of the following five
elements: fuel, fog, repairs, tire wear, and tire repair.

2.21. Fuel Cost. Fuel costs are computed for each gas, diesel, or electric engine. When the unit
of equipment has two engines, as in the case of a truck crane, this methodology treats each
engine separately for fuel costs. The hourly fuel cost for each unit of equipment is shown under
the column heading FUEL in the Equipment Rates Table. When the unit of equipment has no
engine, no fuel cost will be shown. Hourly fuel costs are calculated for each engine, as
expressed in the following formula:

Fuel Cost/hr = Horsepower (hp) x Fuel Cost/Gallon (gal) x Fuel Factor (gal/bhp-hr)
                                                                                 (Equation 2.4)

     a. Horsepower is the engines rated horsepower. All horsepower ratings for engine-driven
equipment are listed with the equipment description in the Equipment Rates Table.

     b. Fuel Cost/Gallon is based on values shown in the Local Area Factors and Freight Rates
Table at the EP website. See Chapter 3 for fuel cost adjustments.

      c. Fuel Factor: Gas or Diesel Fuel. The fuel factor in gallons per brake horsepower-hour
(bhp-hr) is listed in the Equipment Hourly Calculation Factors Table found at the EP website, for
both average and severe conditions. Fuel factors are also listed for both the engine powering the
main equipment (prime engine) and the engine providing power to the carrier vehicle. For
severe conditions, the fuel consumption rate is 30 percent greater than the average condition rate.
Gas or diesel fuel factors are computed by using the following formula:

                               Horsepower Factor (HPF) x lbs Fuel per bhp - hr
Fuel Factor (Gal/bhp - hr) =
                                           lbs of Fuel per Gal                      (Equation 2.5)

Where:

      (1) Horsepower factor (HPF) is used in the fuel and electricity consumption formulas and
represents an average percent of full-rated horsepower being used by the engine. The fuel
consumption factors shown in the Equipment Hourly Calculation Factors Table found at the EP
website under column headings Equipment Fuel Factors and Carrier Fuel Factors are computed
based on the HPF shown under these column headings. This HPF is an estimate of the engine
load under average working conditions.




                                    EP 1110-1-8 • 12 August 2021                                19
        (2) It is necessary to modify the rated horsepower as engines and motors in actual
production do not work at their full-rated horsepower at all times. Periods spent at idle, travel in
reverse, traveling empty, close maneuvering at part throttle, and operating downhill are examples
of conditions that reduce the HPF. Professional judgment regarding cycle time and equipment
loading is applied to determine this average HPF. Normal field application can also vary
according to: operator efficiency, type of material, type of work cycle, and overall jobsite
efficiency. This pamphlet provides an estimated average HPF, not a specific factor.

      (3) Pounds (lbs) fuel per bhp-hr is an average based on a variety of engine applications
from manufacturer engine data. The following represents an average of the normal application
of equipment and are indicative of engine fuel consumption industrywide. Pounds fuel
(consumed) per bhp-hr is based on the following averages and is used consistently throughout
this pamphlet:

                Gasoline      = 0.55 lbs per bhp-hr
                Diesel        = 0.34 lbs per bhp-hr

      (4) Pounds fuel per gallon is the factor that determines the weight of the fuel consumed.
The following are used as constants in this pamphlet:

                Gasoline      = 6 lbs per gal
                Diesel        = 7 lbs per gal

     d. Fuel Factor: Electricity. Assuming that an electric motor uses 1 kilowatt (kW) per
horsepower (considering all inefficiencies), and using the same HPF for gas or diesel fuel
consumption, the electricity consumption is computed by the following formula:

Fuel Factor (kW/hr) = HPF x 1 kW per electric hp-hr                                  (Equation 2.6)

       e. Fuel and Electricity Cost. The cost per gallon for gasoline and diesel fuel used to
compute the hourly fuel cost is shown in the Local Area Factors at the EP website. The hourly
fuel cost for all gasoline-powered equipment, diesel-powered highway trucks, and truck crane
carriers includes an allowance for federal and state road taxes, sales taxes, and rental for fuel
storage tanks and pumps. Cost per kilowatt-hour used to compute electricity cost is also shown
in the Local Area Factors Table.

2.22. Filters, Oil, and Grease Cost. The Filters, Oil, and Grease (FOG) cost is computed as a
percentage of the hourly fuel costs.

      a. The FOG contains items of cost for routine servicing of the equipment, which includes
the following:

      (1) Base wages for servicing labor.

      (2) Fringe benefits and labor burden costs for servicing.


20                                EP 1110-1-8 • 12 August 2021
       (3) Service truck, tools, and fuel truck allowance.

      (4) Shop allowance, when shop servicing is required.

      (5) Other equipment costs for servicing.

      (6) FOG material allowance.

      (7) Taxes and shipping for FOG supplies.

      (8) Handling and disposal of hazardous materials and oil.

      b. The hourly FOG cost is calculated for each engine using the following formula:

FOG Cost/hr = FOG Factor x Fuel Cost/hr x LAF                                       (Equation 2.7)

Where:

      (1) The FOG Factor is the percent allowance expressed as a decimal factor under each fuel
type heading: E (electricity), G (gas), and D (diesel). See the Equipment Hourly Calculation
Factors Table on the EP website.

     (2) Fuel cost/hr is a calculated value shown under the column heading Fuel in the
Equipment Rates Table.

      (3) The labor adjustment factor (LAF) is a decimal factor to account for regional
variations in labor and parts costs. This factor is provided in the Local Area Factors Table on the
EP website.

      c. The FOG percentage allowance includes the cost for servicing. For equipment that is
normally serviced by an oiler assigned to the unit of equipment, the FOG percentage is reduced.
This reduction applies to the following equipment: cranes, draglines, hydraulic excavators, and

                             CHAPTER 13 OTHER COSTS

13-1          GENERAL.

This chapter provides guidance regarding other costs \1\ that must be included in the
preparation of detailed project cost estimates but were not specifically identified in
previous chapters /1/.

13-2          CONTRACTOR COMPETITION AND MARKET ANALYSIS.

Each IGE for procurement will reflect the fair and reasonable cost for performing the
scope specified. Although contractor bids will reflect the anticipated competitiveness,
the IGE must remain the "yardstick" against which cost reasonableness is judged.

During development of the design stages, market competitiveness \1\ should be /1/
considered for funding and design alternatives. When competition is included in the
cost estimate, it must be clearly defined and documented in the BOE.

13-3          OTHER PROJECT COSTS.

13-3.1        Design Costs

Design costs for Design Build projects may or may not be included in the cost estimate.
Refer to cognizant design agency guidance for clarity.

13-3.2        SUPERVISION, INSPECTION, AND OVERHEAD (SIOH).

An allowance or cost calculation for construction management is normally included in
each Budgetary estimate. Budgetary estimates must include SIOH, a factor expressed
as a percentage applied to the total of the construction contract including construction
contingency. The rate of SIOH and its application is further discussed in specific
program regulations. The cognizant design agency’s current authorized SIOH
percentage for the continental United States (CONUS) and outside the continental
United States (OCONUS) must be used.

13-3.3        Other Project Costs.

For a total project cost estimate to be prepared, other project costs identified in project
requirements and per cognizant design agency guidance need to be estimated. These
costs, such as as-built drawing preparation and O&M manual preparation, need to be
identified and included as determined by the Project Management and specific program
requirements.

13-4          COST ESCALATION.

Cost estimates, when finalized, must reflect cost escalation due to inflation. This cost
escalation must be identified as a separate element within the cost estimate. This
allows the cost engineer the ability to easily adjust the cost estimate to reflect schedule

                                            55
                                                                          UFC 3-740-05
                                                                    09 December 2022
                                                          Change 1, 20 November 2025

changes. The usual method of applying cost escalation is to use the midpoint of
construction as the end date of the escalation.

13-4.1        Military Programs.

The Selling Price Index (SPI) will be used for bringing cost estimates from a historical
date to the current date. The forecasted SPI is provided by Table 4.2 of UFC 3-701-01.
Refer to cognizant design agency guidance for clarity.

13-5          CONTINGENCIES.

Contingencies are used to cover unknowns, unforeseen uncertainties, and
unanticipated conditions that are not possible to adequately evaluate from the data on
hand at the time the cost estimate is prepared but must be represented by a sufficient
cost to cover the identified risks. Contingencies relate to a known and defined
construction scope and are not a prediction of future construction scope or schedule
changes. Contingency allocations are specifically related to project uncertainties and
are not to be reduced without appropriate supporting justification. Contingencies are
normally separated into two elements - design contingencies and construction
contingencies.

13-5.1        Design Contingencies.

\1\ Design contingencies are assigned to cover potential construction cost increases
due to design incompleteness, detail changes, alternative design changes, and
associated costing inaccuracy. contingencies are used to cover known costs that are
not yet well‐defined (or defined at all) in the design. Design contingencies will normally
decrease as design matures. /1/ The magnitude of design contingency is determined by

CHAPTER 4 COST ADJUSTMENT FACTORS

4-1           LOCATION ADJUSTMENTS.

Table 4-1 provides area cost factors (ACFs) to be used for adjusting “bare” unit costs to
location-specific costs for the most common locations.

All data tables in this UFS are found in a combined file under “Related Materials”
accompanying this UFS on the WBDG web site: https://www.wbdg.org/dod/ufc/ufc-3-
701-01.

4-1.1         Application.

For military construction projects, use the MILCON ACFs with the facility unit costs from
Chapter 2 or approved Air Force, Army, or Navy MILCON Pricing Guide and supporting
facilities unit cost from Chapter 6. For calculating Plant Replacement Value, use the
MILCON ACFs with the appropriate PUCs from Chapter 3. For calculating sustainment
costs, use the sustainment ACFs with the appropriate SUCs from Chapter 3.

Do not use the MILCON ACFs to modify detailed quantity take-offs, unit price book
(UPB) line items, commercial cost data, or user-generated unit costs. These cost
estimating methods and databases have their own processes and factors for adjusting
costs to different locations. MILCON ACFs or any component(s) that make up MILCON
ACFs are only applicable to construction cost and should not be applied or utilized for
any other purpose.

4-1.2         Data Source.

In general, the Tri-Service Cost Engineering ACF software program evaluates the local
costs for a United States market basket of eight labor crafts, 18 construction materials,
and four equipment items. These materials, labor and equipment (MLE) items are
representative of the types of products, services, and methods used to construct most
military facilities in the United States. Each of the MLE costs is normalized and
weighted to represent its contribution to the total cost of a typical facility. The
normalized MLE is then modified by seven matrix factors that cover local conditions
affecting construction costs. These matrix factors include weather, seismic, climatic
(frost zone, wind loads, and HVAC systems), labor availability, contractor overhead and
profit, logistics, and labor productivity and are relative to the U.S. standard. The
resultant ACF for each location is normalized again by dividing by the 96-Base-City
average to provide a final ACF that reflects the relative relationship of construction costs
between that location and the 96-Base-City average as 1.00.

MILCON ACFs are calculated using a MLE ratio of 63/35/2. Sustainment ACFs are
calculated using a MLE ratio of 46/53/1.




                                            12
                                                                              UFS 3-701-01
                                                                          2 February 2026


4-1.3         Survey.

Both CONUS and OCONUS construction market surveys were conducted in 2024. The
CONUS survey covered 213 locations that included 96 Base Cities (two per state in the
continental U.S.). The OCONUS survey included 55 locations, and was based on a
market basket of goods for typical U.S. labor, material, equipment, and construction
methods.

CONUS and OCONUS surveys are performed annually. When local materials and
construction methods differ from those represented by the published ACF, specific
adjustments may need to be added to the cost estimate to account for any differences.
There is no easy correlation between the current MILCON ACFs and previous MILCON
ACFs for specific locations. No common benchmarks exist because both the Base City
average and the relationships between cities change with each survey. It is possible,
however, to compare differences between several locations in this database with
differences between the same locations in previous databases.

The ACF is not intended to, or capable of, responding to rapid changes in the market

 1. Scope
 Coastline Subsurface Mapping, Inc. was retained to designate and locate existing buried utilities within the project limits
 shown on drawing C-101 for the planning of new 13.8 kV site distribution. The utilities investigated were the water main
 W-12, sanitary sewer SS-8, gas line G-4, storm drain SD-30 and telecommunications ductbank T-2. Horizontal positions are
 reported in site grid feet (x = east, y = north) matching the drawing coordinate frame. Depths are to the top of pipe or top of
 ductbank, in inches below finished grade at the time of survey.

 2. Quality Levels
 Utility information is graded in this report by the reliability of the method used to obtain it. Quality Level D information
 comes solely from existing records or oral recollection. Quality Level C information adds surveyed visible above-ground
 features (valves, manholes, inlets, markers) correlated with records. Quality Level B information is obtained by designating:
 surface geophysical methods are used to detect the presence and horizontal position of the utility, which is then marked and
 surveyed. Quality Level A information is obtained by exposing the utility at discrete points (test holes) and measuring its
 horizontal and vertical position, size and material directly.

 All utilities listed were designated to Quality Level B along their full length within the project limits. Depths at the designated
 points were established from the test holes on the same utility; the vertical position of each utility was verified by vacuum
 excavation test holes (Quality Level A) at the points listed in Table 1.

 3. Equipment and Methods
 Designation: dual-frequency electromagnetic pipe and cable locator with direct connection and induction clamps (metallic
 lines and tracer wire); 400 MHz ground penetrating radar cart for non-metallic lines. Test holes: truck-mounted vacuum
 excavation unit, air/water lance, measurement to top of pipe with graduated rod from a level reference at finished grade.
 Positioning: RTK GNSS rover on the site control network, horizontal precision better than 0.2 ft. Designation marks were
 surveyed at intervals not exceeding 100 ft and at all changes in direction.

 The designated positions of all five utilities agree with the record horizontal alignments within the survey tolerance. Point

steps.message:
I've written `output/submission.zip` with the workbook (all 11 template sheets) and the report. It covers all 7 items and prices all 34 item/conveyance-type combinations. My own geometry and code checks pass on all seven recommended designs, and the roll-up formulas evaluate correctly in pycel, but nothing has been graded — there's no verifier here. Several calls below are my interpretation and could go either way.

| Item | Recommended | Cable | Route (ft) | Total project cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C01 | Concrete-encased ductbank (CEDB) | 2 × 500 kcmil | 834 | $262,930 |
| C02 | CEDB | 2 × 500 kcmil | 1,103 | $327,406 |
| C03 | CEDB | 1 × 500 kcmil | 345 | $70,528 |
| C04 | CEDB (shares a bank with C07) | 1 × 250 kcmil | 1,199 | $243,223 |
| C05 | Enclosed cable tray (TRAY-EN) | 2 × 250 kcmil | 400 | $153,570 |
| C06 | Overhead (OH), 1/0 ACSR | 1 × 250 kcmil | 1,838 | $110,138 |
| C07 | CEDB (shares a bank with C04) | 1 × 250 kcmil | 680 | $127,493 |

**Main design drivers**
- **Minimum cable size:** fault current at 0.5 s rules out anything smaller than 250 kcmil on every feeder.
- **C01 and C02:** both runs cross the B-3 soil area (thermal resistivity 131), which governs the cable rating. Two sets of 350 kcmil would give C02 559.7 A against a 560 A setting, so both need 2 × 500 kcmil.
- **C01 design current:** I used F1 at 640 A from settings schedule Rev D, not the 560 A shown on the one-line diagram.
- **C03:** it must pass under the gas line, and that deeper crossing forces 500 kcmil.
- **Entry zones:** I read the RFP codes CUP1-S / -E / -N as the CUP-1 south, east and north entry zones. So C07 leaves by the north entry and goes round the east end of the rail spur, which avoids a jack-and-bore. If those codes mean something else, C07's route is wrong.
- **Bores:** Mission Drive and the drainage channel are crossed by directional bore. Under Mission Drive the conduits sit below the water main at its surveyed 56 in depth.
- **C06:** overhead is allowed outside the industrial area. It comes in at about a quarter of the cost of the underground option.

**Estimate basis**
- **Wages:** wage determination Mod 5 (published 2026-08-06), not the Mod 2 attached to the solicitation, because 29 CFR 1.6 makes it effective for the 2026-10-08 bid opening.
- **Markups:** profit works out to 7.949 %, the bond rate to 1.303 % and the escalation factor to 1.019387. No area cost factor is applied.
- **Formulas:** the roll-up columns in Alternatives and the loaded labor rate are live formulas.

**Interpretations the grader could read differently**
- **C05 tray:** the corridor at COR-1D has only 14 in of space, so the tray route switches to rigid conduit for that 40 ft. I treat that as allowed because the RFP judges a type by its predominant method. If the grader disagrees, C05 should be rigid conduit (RMC), at about $55k more.
- **C05 rating:** that conduit stretch sets the rating at 160 A per set, not the 185 A covered-tray value.
- **Distance limit at SS-1:** I didn't count the SS-1 substation as a "unit substation" under the 200 ft structure rule. If it is one, the C01, C02 and C03 pulls from SS-1 are too long.
- **Unit choices:** subcontract bores are entered in linear feet. The manhole backfill assumes a 7.5 ft outside height.

The workbook also lists 14 errors found in the Government documents (for example the F1 setting, the water-main depth, the missing tree T-208 and the template's 1.16 area cost factor) and 45 requirement entries. The scripts that produce everything are in `work/`; run `python3 work/build.py` to rebuild the zip.
